definition: In computer science, a ball tree, balltree or metric tree, is a space partitioning data structure for organizing points in a multi-dimensional space.
details: A ball tree partitions data points into a nested set of balls. The resulting data structure has characteristics that make it useful for a number of applications, most notably nearest neighbor search.

explainer.lead: A ball tree organizes points in a multidimensional space by placing them inside nested balls. This structure is especially useful for nearest-neighbor search, where the goal is to find points close to a chosen point.

tiers.eli5: Imagine drawing circles around clusters of marbles, then drawing bigger circles around several of those circles. A ball tree does something similar with points, including points that have more dimensions than we can draw. The nested circles help a computer look for nearby points.
tiers.practitioner: Use a ball tree to index multidimensional points when nearest-neighbor search is a central operation. The data structure partitions the points into nested balls, producing a hierarchy that the search can use. Its defining feature is this ball-based partitioning, not a particular search application or software package.
tiers.paperLevel: A ball tree, also called a balltree or metric tree, is a space-partitioning data structure that organizes points in a multidimensional space into a nested set of balls. Its principal application is nearest-neighbor search.

explainer.example: For a collection of points on a map, place nearby points inside small balls, then place those small balls inside larger regional balls. The resulting hierarchy organizes all the points and can support a nearest-neighbor search.

usedIn.name: Nearest-neighbor search
usedIn.detail: Uses the nested-ball organization to support searches for nearby points.

usedIn.name: Multidimensional point organization
usedIn.detail: Partitions points in a multidimensional space into a useful hierarchy.

explainer.intuition: Instead of keeping all points in one unstructured collection, enclose groups of them in balls and enclose those balls in larger balls. The result is a nested organization of the space.
howItWorks: Start with points in a multidimensional space.
Partition the points into groups represented by balls.
Nest smaller balls inside larger balls.
Use the resulting ball tree for tasks such as nearest-neighbor search.
explainer.whyItMatters: Ball trees give multidimensional points a useful structure rather than leaving them as an unorganized collection. Their most notable benefit is supporting nearest-neighbor search.
misconceptions: A ball tree is not a flat grouping: its balls are nested.
It is a data structure, not the nearest-neighbor search itself.
